extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of personal/reflective essays; educated general readers interested in reading, writing, and judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and philosophical guidance for reading books and composing personal essays: how to choose what to read, how to borrow and use authorities, the proper temper and method of writing, and standards of judgment and humility for authors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on method over matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Let none lay stress upon the matter I write, but upon my method in writing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should evaluate the work primarily by the author's method and manner of writing, not by the absolute novelty or authority of the factual matter. Observe what is borrowed and whether those borrowings are chosen to 'raise or help the invention' (i.e., to serve the author's method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek knowledge where it is to be found
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever goes in quest of knowledge, let him fish for it where it is to be found; there is nothing I so little profess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue expertise in the proper sources rather than pretending broad authority; acknowledge the limits of one's own competence and go to specialists or established authorities for specific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write as self-revelation, not authoritative discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: These are fancies of my own, by which I do not pretend to discover things but to lay open myself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayist's aim is to expose and examine his own thoughts and disposition rather than to produce definitive didactic treatises; evaluate such writing as candid self-inquiry rather than authoritative doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective borrowing: weigh, not number
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not number my borrowings, I weigh them; and had I designed to raise their value by number, I had made them twice as many; they are all... so famed and ancient authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer quality and relevance of quotations/citations over quantity. Choose authorities that genuinely support or enrich the thought rather than amassing names to impress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authorities to shelter or challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: In reasons, comparisons, and arguments, if I transplant any into my own soil... I purposely conceal the author, to awe the temerity of those precipitate censors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author may invoke or obscure sources for rhetorical effect—either to protect his weakness under established reputations or to provoke critics into contesting the authority rather than the author. Be deliberate about attribution as a rhetorical and protective strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession of ignorance as a mark of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The confession of ignorance is one of the finest and surest testimonies of judgment that I know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitting one's limits and uncertainties is a sign of sound judgment and should be valued in both reading and writing; humility is preferable to false display of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read for honest diversion or self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: I seek, in the reading of books, only to please myself by an honest diversion; or, if I study, 'tis for no other science than what treats of the knowledge of myself, and instructs me how to die and how to live well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of reading may legitimately be entertainment or the cultivation of self-understanding and practical wisdom; clarity about one's purpose should guide selection and evaluation of books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon what does not disclose itself quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not bite my nails about the difficulties I meet with in my reading; after a charge or two, I give them over. What I do not discern at once is by persistence rendered more obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a book does not yield understanding with reasonable attention, it may be wiser to set it aside and return later; persistent obstinacy in reading can darken and tire judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read with gaiety; avoid excessive continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: I do nothing without gaiety; continuation and a too obstinate endeavour, darkens, stupefies, and tires my judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a light, cheerful temper in reading and study. Forced, joyless persistence reduces effectiveness and enjoyment—take breaks or change books when weariness sets in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer older works and read in languages you can judge
rubrics_metrics.description: I care not much for new ones, because the old seem fuller and stronger; neither do I converse much with Greek authors, because my judgment cannot do its work with imperfect intelligence of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older established works often have more depth; avoid critiquing writings in languages you do not sufficiently master, because imperfect understanding undermines sound judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borrowed material must serve original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Let them observe, in what I borrow, if I have known how to choose what is proper to raise or help the invention, which is always my own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotations and sources to amplify or clarify your own thought; borrowed elements should support, not replace, the author's original contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value clarity, force, and beauty of discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall love any one that can unplume me, that is, by clearness of understanding and judgment, and by the sole distinction of the force and beauty of the discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate writing by its clarity, the strength of its reasoning, and the beauty (or aesthetic force) of its expression; these are higher merits than empty rhetoric or mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be self-critical and avoid over-responsibility for one's writings
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever shall catch me tripping in ignorance, will not in any sort get the better of me; for I should be very unwilling to become responsible to another for my writings, who am not so to myself, nor satisfied with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be ready to accept critique and not proffer their work as infallible; personal dissatisfaction with one’s own writing is preferable to false claims of completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow local custom and law in distributing goods (wills)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, the most judicious distribution of our goods, when we come to die, is, in my opinion, to let them be distributed according to the custom of the country; the laws have considered the matter better than we know how to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a will or choosing heirs, prefer established legal/customary rules over whimsical personal rearrangements except for great and manifest cause; avoid letting transient passions determine permanent dispositions.
